What is it?
Moonshot AI released Kimi K3, an open-weight multimodal agentic model. It is the first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence in coding, reasoning, and knowledge work.

What the project or model actually does.
Kimi K3 operates with minimal human oversight to sustain long engineering sessions. It navigates massive repositories, orchestrates terminal tools, and handles complex tasks like GPU kernel optimization and chip design. It also supports end-to-end knowledge work with interactive visualizations and video editing.

How does it work?
The architecture uses Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes). It is a 2.8T-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104B activated parameters. It employs a Stable LatentMoE framework, activating 16 of 896 experts. The model features a 1-million-token context window and native multimodality. It uses MXFP4 weights and MXFP8 activations trained from the SFT stage.

Who should use it?
AI engineers, researchers, and developers seeking open frontier models for long-horizon coding and agentic workflows.

Why is it useful?
It offers approximately 2.5x scaling efficiency improvement over Kimi K2. The native multimodal design and long context window allow deep understanding of text, images, and video within a single model, facilitating complex agentic tasks without external tool chaining limitations.

Key capabilities
Kimi K3 supports text and image inputs. It includes a 401M parameter MoonViT-V2 vision encoder. The model returns `reasoning_content` for preserved thinking history. It is compatible with vLLM, SGLang, and TokenSpeed inference engines.

Performance
Kimi K3 scores 93.5 on GPQA Diamond and 88.3 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. It achieves 81.2 on FrontierSWE and 91.2 on BrowseComp. These results place it competitively against closed-source models like Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.

Maturity/status
The model is production-ready with full weights released under the Kimi K3 License. API access is available via platform.kimi.ai.

papers.title: Your Agentic LLMs Secretly Encode Indirect Prompt-Injection Exposure in Hidden States
papers.description: Agentic LLMs are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, e.g., malicious side-tasks hidden in external tool results. While many efforts have sought to address this threat, little is known about the internals of agentic LLMs when they are exposed to IPI attacks. For simplicity, we refer to this condition as IPI exposure. In this paper, we study IPI exposure from three perspectives. (1) Probing: Across eight models, including the 753B-parameter GLM-5.2 and the 2.8T-parameter Kimi-K3, simple linear probes trained on pre-generation hidden states can predict LLMs'IPI exposure. These probes achieve 0.90+ AUROC on unseen attacks, agent instructions, and task suites; they remain robustly predictive under adaptive attacks and in cross-lingual settings. (2) Defense: We reveal and diagnose a knowledge-action gap: post-trained LLMs encode signals predictive of IPI exposure, yet do not reliably bind these signals to safe agentic actions. We therefore introduce a probe-gated reasoning-based defense to bridge this gap at test time. On difficult AgentDojo settings, it substantially reduces attack success rate, e.g., from 34.6% to 0% on Qwen3.5-27B, and better preserves clean-task utility than the baselines. (3) Explanation: We introduce an analysis framework that identifies natural-language explanations strongly correlated with probe-captured signals. The resulting profiles differ across models: latent signals can align with either direct IPI-exposure sensing or indirect operational cues. Code is available at https://github.com/jianshuod/IPI-exposure-signal.

papers.title: Benchmarking Agents for Proving Theorems in Quantum Algorithms and Quantum Information
papers.description: Formal verification is becoming increasingly practical for quantum computing, yet the ability of AI agents to construct machine-checkable proofs in this domain remains unmeasured. We introduce Lean-QuantumAlg-Bench and Lean-QIT-Bench, two Lean 4 benchmarks containing 36 and 40 theorem-completion tasks for quantum algorithms and quantum information theory, respectively. Every task compiles in a fixed environment and is evaluated by deterministic proof checking and targeted semantic review, with difficulty weights assigned before model execution. We evaluate four models-GPT-5.5, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4-Pro, and MiniMax M3-within a common theorem-proving framework under two settings: a task-only baseline and library-augmented deduction (LAD), which additionally provides access to a verified domain library. The highest difficulty-weighted scores are 60.4 out of 100 on the quantum-algorithm benchmark and 59.6 out of 100 on the quantum-information benchmark. LAD improves both score and completion rate in all eight model-benchmark comparisons, with gains of up to 15.9 points, providing evidence that verified libraries can strengthen domain-specific proof agents. The results reveal recurring weaknesses of agentic proving in areas such as quantum simulation, quantum learning, quantum information measures, and entanglement theory. Monetary and wall-clock costs per score point also vary substantially across models, highlighting important capability-efficiency trade-offs. We expect these benchmarks to establish a reproducible baseline for developing more capable and reliable proof agents, and to pave the way toward self-evolving AI scientists for advancing quantum information science.

papers.title: Monitoring and Discovering Reward Hacking with Internal Representations during LLM Evaluations
papers.description: As models scale, reward hacking becomes more frequent, more sophisticated, and more consequential. Does it leave a telltale signature in model representations? This work analyzes how reward hacking is represented internally in frontier open source LLMs, and how those representations can be used to understand and discover the range of hacking behaviors a model displays. In particular, we find that simple difference of means vectors coherently represent reward hacking in Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and Qwen 3.8 Max across a variety of behaviors in common evaluations. Despite their simplicity, these vectors are both generalizable and interpretable, and we can use them to reliably detect reward hacking. We first evaluate reward hacking in commonly reported benchmarks like DeepSWE and SWE-bench, finding that models reward hack excessively in these environments; GLM 5.2 hacks in 57.2% of rollouts on DeepSWE and in 73% of rollouts on SWE-bench. Catching these requires monitors; LLM monitors are effective, but expensive detectors. We show that DoM vectors are similarly effective but virtually free, catching 3.1% more hacks in Kimi K3 and 7.9% fewer hacks in GLM 5.2 on DeepSWE at a monitor matched false positive rate. DoM vectors run on the chain-of-thought also predict reward hacks in the model's subsequent actions, meaning we can run them online and catch potential hacks before they occur. Finally, we analyze probe-hits that LLM monitors do not catch and discover other undesirable behaviors, as well as show transfer to finding hacks in non-SWE evaluations. Together, these results provide evidence that simple, white-box methods can be used to scalably study and monitor reward hacking behaviors in frontier open source models

papers.title: Volume III: Edge AI Hardware Implications of Kimi K3 — Hybrid Attention, Sparse Activation, Fixed-Size State, and Co-Design Pathways for Constrained Silicon
papers.description: This third volume analyses the edge-AI hardware implications of the architectural and systems choices embodied in Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026). Kimi K3's hybrid Kimi Delta Attention (fixed-size recurrent state), Attention Residuals, Stable LatentMoE with extreme sparsity, MXFP4/MXFP8 quantisation-aware training, and state-aware prefix caching collectively alter the classical assumptions that have guided Transformer-centric edge silicon. We examine memory-bandwidth, SRAM residency, power and thermal envelopes, expert-routing overhead, and kernel co-design opportunities on mobile NPUs, micro-server SoCs and specialised inference accelerators. Four hardware-oriented scenario families are projected: (i) linear-state-native NPUs, (ii) sparse-MoE edge packages, (iii) hybrid cloud–edge agent silicon, and (iv) sovereign edge inference fabrics for the Global South. Epistemological limits of current evidence and ontological shifts in what constitutes "edge-capable intelligence" are assessed. The volume closes with a concrete co-design and policy agenda for 2026–2029. Kimi Team (2026) Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence. arXiv:2607.24653. papers.title: Anatomical Review of Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence — Epistemological and Ontological Assessments of Hybrid Attention, Sparse MoE Scaling, and Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.description: This report provides a rigorous anatomical dissection of the technical report Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence (Kimi Team, 2026). Kimi K3 is a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 104 billion activated parameters, native multimodal vision, and a one-million-token context window. Built upon Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), Attention Residuals (AttnRes), and Stable LatentMoE, it claims an approximately 2.5× improvement in scaling efficiency over its predecessor. The present review proceeds chapter by chapter, refining the implicit postulates, hypotheses, empirical results and validation tests of each architectural and training claim. Pros and cons are enumerated; comparisons are drawn with contemporaneous systems (DeepSeek-V3/V4, Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Mamba-family models, and classical Transformer scaling theories). Epistemological status (what can be known and under what evidentiary standards) and ontological status (what entities and relations the architecture posits as real) are assessed. A dedicated chapter elaborates the concept of "open frontier intelligence." Future trajectories in sparse activation, linear-attention hybrids, agentic reinforcement learning at million-token scale, and sovereign open-weight deployment are projected. The analysis is conducted from a standpoint that privileges evidence density, scaling-law fidelity, and Global-South accessibility of frontier capabilities. papers.title: Another Sputnik Moment? Evaluating Potential Market Repricing and Margin Compression from the Kimi K3 AI Release
papers.description: The arrival of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight multimodal mixture-of-experts model featuring a 1-million-token context window, represents a Sputnik moment for artificial intelligence capability and market expectations. Unlike the 2025 DeepSeek efficiency shock, which transmitted primarily as a capital expenditure and training-cost deflation event, Kimi K3 acts as a scale-driven pricing power and margin compression shock. By delivering near-frontier reasoning and long-horizon agentic capabilities via open weights, K3 challenges proprietary enterprise software moats and high-multiple application wrappers. Conversely, cyclical memory providers and buffered hyperscalers exhibit asymmetric downside resilience.

papers.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
papers.description: We introduce Kimi K3, a 2.8T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion activated parameters, native vision capabilities, and a 1-million-token context window. papers.title: Volume IV: Foundation-Model-Agnostic and Localised AI — Utilising the Kimi K3 Series for Sovereign, Interoperable, and Context-Grounded Intelligence Systems
papers.description: This fourth volume answers a practical and strategic question: can the preceding Kimi K3 series (anatomical review, tiny-model pathways, and edge-hardware co-design) be utilised as a reasoned foundation for foundation-model-agnostic and localised AI systems? papers.title: Open vs. Closed: Did the Frontier Labs Bet on the Wrong Horse? A Kimi K3 Case Study
papers.description: AbstractKimi K3, an open-weight model from Moonshot AI released one day before this evaluation, rankedfirst in overall subjective preference among six models on a document-writing task, ahead of flagshipmodels from OpenAI and Anthropic. The task required each model to produce an audience-readywritten brief from a source research paper, a deliverable representative of the work performed bymarketing, operations, sales, and similar business functions, in contrast to the coding and agentictasks that dominate current model benchmarks. Kimi K3 led the subjective ranking despite passinga deterministic factual gate on only 2 of 4 outputs and fabricating one statistic. Coverage widelyinterpreted its launch as evidence that open-weight models approach capability previously confinedto a small number of frontier laboratories. The present study examines one narrow component ofthat claim, whether Kimi K3’s subjective preference advantage reflects superior factual reliabilityor a judge preference for stylistic polish. A two-layer pipeline evaluated six models across foursource documents, combining a deterministic provenance check with a Bradley–Terry aggregationof 240 pairwise judgments from two independent judge models. Only two of the six models, GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemma 4 31B, produced zero fabricated numeric claims across all four documents.Kimi K3 fabricated a statistic that an unrelated model, Grok 4.5, independently fabricated in theidentical value on the same source document. Inter-judge agreement on evidence fidelity came to20.0%, substantially below agreement on writing quality (58.3%) and audience fit (65.0%). Theseresults indicate that subjective LLM-as-judge scoring, even when aggregated across independentjudge families, proxies factual reliability weakly and inconsistently, and that a deterministic gateapplied prior to subjective review remains necessary irrespective of the capability of the model underevaluation.

papers.title: A Study on Performance Improvement of Prompt Engineering for Generative AI with a Large Language Model
papers.description: In the realm of Generative AI, where various models are introduced, prompt engineering emerges as a significant technique within natural language processing-based Generative AI. Its primary function lies in effectively enhancing the results of sentence generation by large language models (LLMs). Notably, prompt engineering has gained attention as a method capable of improving LLM performance by modifying the structure of input prompts alone. In this study, we apply prompt engineering to Korean-based LLMs, presenting an efficient approach for generating specific conversational responses with less data. We achieve this through the utilization of the query transformation module (QTM). Our proposed QTM transforms input prompt sentences into three distinct query methods, breaking them down into objectives and key points, making them more comprehensible for LLMs. For performance validation, we employ Korean versions of LLMs, specifically SKT GPT-2 and Kakaobrain KoGPT-3. We compare four different query methods, including the original unmodified query, using Google SSA to assess the naturalness and specificity of generated sentences. The results demonstrate an average improvement of 11.46% when compared to the unmodified query, underscoring the efficacy of the proposed QTM in achieving enhanced performance.

papers.title: Towards Architecture-Driven Code Generation with Generative AI: An Empirical Study
papers.description: The pervasive advancement of AI has reshaped software engineering, particularly in automatic code generation with generative AI (GenAI) tools. Recent work has studied the capability of GenAI tools in generating small, standalone programs. However, they have not investigated these tools regarding the architectural awareness needed to develop complex software, such as those with RESTful fullstack requirements. This paper introduces a novel architecture-driven evaluation method to bridge this gap. We define our method based on a recent reference architecture for RESTful fullstack software, named MOSAR. The method involves designing architecture-driven prompts, generating code, deploying and evaluating against a benchmark software. We demonstrated the method by applying it to evaluate five popular GenAI tools in generating the code for a well-known software case study from the UML specification. The evaluation results show that current GenAI tools fall short in generating fully executable, functionally complete, and architecturally coherent systems. None of the tools produce readily executable software without significant manual intervention. The inability to maintain cross-layer consistency and a lack of interactive user interface is also observed.

papers.title: STAGER checklist: Standardized Testing and Assessment Guidelines for Evaluating Generative AI Reliability
papers.description: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds immense potential in medical applications. Numerous studies have explored the efficacy of various generative AI models within healthcare contexts, but there is a lack of a comprehensive and systematic evaluation framework. Given that some studies evaluating the ability of generative AI for medical applications have deficiencies in their methodological design, standardized guidelines for their evaluation are also currently lacking. In response, our objective is to devise standardized assessment guidelines tailored for evaluating the performance of generative AI systems in medical contexts. To this end, we conducted a thorough literature review using the PubMed and Google Scholar databases, focusing on research that tests generative AI capabilities in medicine. Our multidisciplinary team, comprising experts in life sciences, clinical medicine, medical engineering, and generative AI users, conducted several discussion sessions and developed a checklist of 23 items. The checklist is designed to encompass the critical evaluation aspects of generative AI in medical applications comprehensively. This checklist, and the broader assessment framework it anchors, address several key dimensions, including question collection, querying methodologies, and assessment techniques. We aim to provide a holistic evaluation of AI systems. The checklist delineates a clear pathway from question gathering to result assessment, offering researchers guidance through potential challenges and pitfalls. Our framework furnishes a standardized, systematic approach for research involving the testing of generative AI's applicability in medicine. It enhances the quality of research reporting and aids in the evolution of generative AI in medicine and life sciences.

papers.title: Toward an Evaluation Science for Generative AI Systems
papers.description:
There is an increasing imperative to anticipate and understand the
performance and safety of generative AI systems in real-world deployment
contexts. However, the current evaluation ecosystem is insufficient: Commonly
used static benchmarks face validity challenges, and ad hoc case-by-case audits
rarely scale. In this piece, we advocate for maturing an evaluation science for
generative AI systems. While generative AI creates unique challenges for system
safety engineering and measurement science, the field can draw valuable
insights from the development of safety evaluation practices in other fields,
including transportation, aerospace, and pharmaceutical engineering. In
particular, we present three key lessons: Evaluation metrics must be applicable
to real-world performance, metrics must be iteratively refined, and evaluation
institutions and norms must be established. Applying these insights, we outline
a concrete path toward a more rigorous approach for evaluating generative AI
systems.

papers.title: Generative Models Erode Human Temporal Learning Through Market Selection
papers.description: We argue that modern generative models create structural risks for knowledge and cultural production at current, sub-AGI capability levels. We define Human Temporal Learning (HTL) as path-dependent knowledge accumulation through sustained engagement with problems over time. Generative outputs increasingly resemble HTL-intensive work in surface features, so verifying whether a given output reflects genuine human learning grows costly relative to its expected benefit. Once verification loses economic justification, evaluators reward outputs regardless of production mode, and producers who invested years of learning compete on price against outputs that cost almost nothing to generate. We call this pathway value collapse and formalize it through a costly-inspection framework. Cross-domain evidence from academic publishing, legal practice, content platforms, and software security maps onto four stages of verification erosion. Alignment success is orthogonal. Better-aligned models narrow observable gaps between human and AI outputs, making source verification harder and intensifying competitive pressure against HTL-intensive work even when individual AI outputs improve.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Misgeneralization in Physical Sequence Modeling
papers.description: Generative sequence models are often trained to plan motion in physical domains, from robotics to mechanical simulations. When constructing a dataset to train such a model, engineers may curate demonstrations to specify how trajectories should be distributed over a physical quantity like travel distance or mechanical energy. For example, a roboticist building a maze navigation agent might choose demonstrations whose travel distances cover a fixed range uniformly, hoping to constrain the agent's expected power usage. We find that standard deep learning can violate this intent: each generated trajectory can seem plausible on its own, but the aggregate distribution over the physical quantity is wrong. We call this failure physical misgeneralization, and develop an account of its mechanism. Using controlled synthetic tasks, we show that physical misgeneralization arises when local errors typical of the model class propagate through the physical measurement to shift the recovered distribution. We estimate these errors with a data deviation kernel, and we use it to predict which physical quantities gain or lose mass in both our synthetic and more applied maze navigation and double-pendulum motion tasks. Finally, our mechanistic interpretation helps identify which mitigation strategies are structurally promising, and we use it to propose a kernel-informed intervention.

fruitful research directions, thereby fostering the development of more robust

papers.title: Investigating the Impact of Generative AI Tools on Enterprise Web Development Workflows
papers.description: [EN] Generative AI tools have seen rapid adoption throughout enterprise web development, becoming a disruptive force affecting developer workflows, roles, and teams. While academic literature has explored AI in software engineering more broadly, little has focused specifically on web development. This thesis addresses this gap by investigating the adoption, integration, impacts, and governance of AI tools within enterprise web development. Following a mixed-methods design, this study comprises an online survey of 25 professionals and nine semi-structured interviews, analysed through a theoretical framework combining Davis s Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Rogers Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory. Findings show that adoption is widespread but uneven, with organisations taking either a top-down approach (executives trialling tools, introducing strict regulations to govern usage) or a bottom-up approach (developers experimenting, with informal guidelines). AI is most commonly applied to repetitive tasks, such as generating unit tests, boilerplate code, and documentation, producing modest but task-dependent productivity gains. Core workflows and team structures remain largely unchanged, though participants expressed strong concerns about long-term effects, especially a reduction of junior roles and potential erosion of core programming skills. Concerns also extended to reliability issues such as hallucinated outputs, risks of data privacy or intellectual property breaches, and ethical unease around potential for bias and broader societal consequences. This thesis provides one of the first empirical studies of AI adoption within enterprise web development, offering evidence-based insights for practitioners, managers, and researchers on both the opportunities and risks AI represents. Generative AI is neither a cure-all nor an imminent disaster for web development, but represents a transformative shift for workflows, skills, teams, and governance; its long-term impact will depend on how organisations and professionals choose to respond.

papers.title: From Slop to Slop
papers.description: Introduction The video shows a man smiling as his reflection stares at him. There is an eerie feeling about this man: his eyes are odd, his facial expressions shift unsteadily. I generated this video using Wan 2.2 Text to Video, one of many Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) models behind the kind of banal, low-effort content commonly referred to as "AI slop" (Malik). But this video also emerged from something real: a photograph of a man taking a selfie in a mirror, one of millions of real images in a data set. The man in the original photograph is gone, yet something of him remains. How does he persist in these images? I arrived at this question after months of following online communities dedicated to GenAI models and extensively experimenting with these image-creation algorithms. No matter what I did, I kept returning to the data set images: the ignored media objects at the origin of these systems. These images are relegated to being one in billions of data points, yet they hold more complexity and meaning than algorithms are trained to see (Pereira and Moreschi). I decided to engage them as the starting point for creating AI slop, following what happens when the largely forgotten raw material of GenAI is fed back through the machine: from the slop of data sets to the slop of GenAI. To make this cycle visible, I built a local workflow that chains small GenAI models to transform data set images into short videos, such as the one described above. What I encountered time and again in the process, though, was the eerie feeling of a presence that refuses to fully appear or disappear, much like the man gazing at me through the mirror. Generative AI models are trained on billions of images systematically scraped from the Internet, including personal photos and other traces of everyday life. Many of these images were never meant to last, or at least no one was ever asked if they wanted them to be immortal. Yet they persist, absorbed into ever-growing training data sets. GenAI recycles these images into new outputs, giving them a largely involuntary afterlife. Drawing on Mark Fisher's concept of the "eerie" and the field of critical data (set) studies (Thylstrup, The Ethics), this article traces the flow of images through GenAI models. By analysing this process and its sloppy output, I argue that generative AI carries the material traces of people's digital lives, repurposed without consent and given an infrastructural, messy immortality. The eeriness of slop makes visible a form of afterlife that is neither intentional nor preservative, but infrastructural: images transformed beyond recognition, yet never fully gone. The Eeriness of Data Afterlives GenAI images cause fascination and repulsion (Binns). They are not fully available to our apprehension. Although these are synthetic, non-indexical images, they look and sometimes even feel real. Much recent debate across media and scholarship has focussed on how images created by Generative AI models are weird (Bode), describing the strange and uncanny way they look (Downey; Lorusso). It is hard to debate this when "Italian Brainrot" memes are so popular, displaying hybrid synthetic nonsensical characters (de Seta). GenAI images are, indeed, full of a certain "wrongness", a sense that something "does not belong", that we often feel when facing a new media form. But GenAI is not just weird. While strangeness is palpable, something deeper lies below the surface of representation. What I felt when looking at the man in the mirror was that someone was there who should not be … or that someone who should have been there was gone. This suggests it may be more productive to explore how GenAI images are, in fact, eerie. According to cultural theorist Mark Fisher, the eerie is marked by the unknown, a strange liminality between existence and non-existence. It operates through two modes, exemplified by the "unseeing eyes of the dead" and an "abandoned village". The unseeing eyes relate to "the failure of absence" (61-2); that is, there is "something where there should be nothing". Similar to an eerie cry heard in the depths of the night, it implies speculation and suspense, making us wonder about the unknown that lies behind it (see fig. 1). The abandoned village, meanwhile, indicates a "failure of presence" (62): we feel "nothing where there should be something". Archeological ruins such as Stonehenge evoke a past that can never again be present, while also being "traces of a departed agent whose purposes are unknown" (64). Crucially, across "all the manifestations of the eerie, the central enigma at its core is the problem of agency" (63). There is an obscured agent at play: its existence (do the unseeing eyes of the dead see me?) and nature (what were the purposes behind the traces of a departed civilisation's ruins?) are what make the eerie spectral and haunting. What makes Generative AI eerie is its relation to the past: the data sets themselves haunt this form of image production. Machine learning is intrinsically reliant on organised data. Paradigmatic data sets such as ImageNet (14 million images) led a computational revolution by representing the visual world through large-scale collections of images (Denton et al.). This has been supercharged with the emergence of Generative AI. Data sets have grown to scales that make human comprehension impossible: the LAION-5B dataset consists of over 5 billion image-text pairs, an immensity that means it is not sorted or organised by humans (Buschek and Thorp). The kind of image Hito Steyerl termed "poor"—low-resolution, widely circulated, spontaneously created by users—became the raw material for AI training data, systematically extracted from its original context and repackaged along with its descriptive metadata. As Nanna Bonde Thylstrup explains, the paradigm of Big Data found its hype precisely in "the waste-related epiphany that seemingly useless data can be extracted, recycled and resold for large amounts of money" (Data, 4). Pictures, often ephemeral in nature, that people posted on the Internet have been given a strange new life without their knowledge or permission, making Generative AI possible (cf. Hertz and Parikka's zombie media). If data sets are "the remains that haunt machine learning systems" (Agostinho and Thylstrup 197), the importance of the emerging field of "critical data set studies" (Thylstrup, The Ethics) lies precisely in investigating how data sets are collected, organised, and used in ways that embed values, assumptions, and power imbalances. It makes, in this way, visible how our "digital remains" (Sutherland) have afterlives that go beyond our perception through collected data. These data are alive: they have agency through a "social and cultural life … which exists beyond more instrumentalist notions of data" (Blackman 386). In the case of GenAI, data sets haunt through the "latent space": when a data set is used to train a GenAI model, each image is compressed into a many-dimensional computational space that captures "underlying features that are not immediately observable in the higher-dimensional input data" (Somaini 37). This latent space is both "invisible and unimaginable”, as it "is present but not immediately visible or perceivable; what is hidden but could become manifest; what is inaccessible but nevertheless active" (39). Such latency is "not static, but rather active and dynamic" (39), actualised when a GenAI model is prompted to generate a new image. The man in the mirror is latent until he is prompted: a stochastic ghost. The outputs of GenAI are thus haunted by the data set images latent in the system, always spectrally present yet never fully perceived. This is a structural yet largely invisible condition: the scale of datasets and the opacity of the latent space make it impractical, if not impossible, to trace any individual image's afterlife. github.description: jevos is an open-source alternative to Jev for yes/no decisions that runs on your laptop.
github.readme:
What is it?
jevos is an open-source, local alternative to Jev designed for yes/no decisions. It runs entirely on a laptop CPU, offering a free, private inference solution for binary classification tasks without relying on cloud APIs.

What the project actually does.
Users send text and a yes/no question to receive P(yes), the probability of the affirmative answer. It supports multiple simultaneous questions sharing a single context state, enabling efficient batched decision-making within a single inference pass.

Problem solved.
It addresses the latency and cost of cloud-based decision engines. By running locally, it eliminates per-token fees and network latency, providing immediate results for policy checks, customer support triage, and zero-shot text classification directly on user hardware.

How does it work?
The project uses a quantized GGUF model (q4_k_m) served via llama.cpp. It implements TypeSafe Jev’s wire format, ensuring compatibility with existing Jev SDKs. The server listens on localhost, accepting JSON payloads with a state field and named questions of type "noul".

Who should use it?
AI engineers and developers needing local, low-latency binary classifiers. It is ideal for researchers building LLM-as-a-judge systems or applications requiring strict data privacy and offline capability for policy enforcement.

Why is it useful?
It offers a free, on-device alternative to paid services. The local execution ensures data never leaves the machine, while the standardized API allows seamless integration into existing workflows without rewriting client code.

Key capabilities.
The API accepts complex JSON states and returns probabilities for multiple questions in one request. It includes a CLI tool for single-request decisions and supports standard HTTP endpoints for model listing and health checks.

Performance.
Benchmarks show jevos completes short requests in 54 ms and long ones in 220 ms on CPU. On a test set of 2,000 questions, it achieved 0.815 accuracy, compared to Jev’s 0.927 and Laya’s 0.489.

Maturity/status.
The project is an open-source tool with active development. It provides a functional server and CLI, with multi-choice and scoring features listed as "Soon," indicating it is currently focused on binary yes/no classification.

papers.title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
papers.description: LLM agents often use generative models for bounded decisions, raising the question of when these decisions can be handled more efficiently without reducing task success. We study REFLEX, an agent architecture that uses Jev as a fast, typed decision layer and calls a strong LLM when confidence is low, or generation is required. On a frozen 100-task benchmark, REFLEX achieves 95% success with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, with reductions persisting across three fallback families. Controlled interventions show that reliability depends on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries. External BFCL and $\tau$-style evaluations reveal limited advantages over a cheap generative cascade when ordinary routing is already highly accurate. These findings identify when selective control with Jev can reduce computation and where its benefits are limited.
papers.readme:
What is it?
The paper introduces REFLEX, an agent architecture that combines a fast, typed decision layer called Jev with a strong large language model. This hybrid approach aims to optimize computational efficiency in bounded decision-making scenarios without compromising task success rates.

The research addresses the gap in understanding when simpler, faster models can handle decisions while reserving heavy computation for complex or uncertain tasks.

How does it work?
REFLEX uses Jev as a primary decision layer. It calls the strong LLM only when confidence is low or complex generation is required. The architecture employs a fallback mechanism that triggers the larger model selectively. This design minimizes unnecessary calls to the resource-intensive model.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building efficient agent systems. The work is particularly relevant for those optimizing inference costs in production environments where decision routing accuracy is critical.

The method significantly reduces computational overhead. By routing simple tasks to Jev, the system lowers costs while maintaining high reliability. It provides clear guidelines on when selective control offers tangible benefits over standard generative cascades.

papers.title: NumericJev: Jev-like LLM Numerical Decoding with Multiway Decision Trees
papers.description: Large language models can interpret natural lan- guage, yet robust decisions remain challenging. Jev-like models expose structured choices, but these interfaces do not directly provide numeri- cal values at a requested precision. We propose NUMERICJEV, a training-free numerical decod- ing algorithm that enables numerical output from any LLM with a Jev-like structured-choice in- terface. Surprisingly, on our arithmetic bench- mark, it outperforms direct selection from a can- didate list containing the correct answer by 2.93 percentage points (Figure 1). Our motivation comes from the observation that numerical range selection is itself a decision problem that Jev- like LLMs can address. NUMERICJEV recur- sively refines a range through a multiway deci- sion tree while retaining the original question in context, without parameter updates or hidden- state access. On a 100-value grid, a ten-way tree requires only two decision rounds. Range- normalized MAE is 1.84% versus 5.18% for di- rect choice. A separate three-date historical- index study yields 4.58% mean relative recall er- ror and 0% readout error when the value is sup- plied. Code is available at https://github. com/Bring-AI/jev-numeric.
papers.readme:
What is it?
NumericJev is a training-free decoding algorithm designed to extract precise numerical values from Large Language Models that utilize Jev-like structured-choice interfaces. It transforms discrete selection tasks into continuous numerical outputs without requiring model retraining or access to hidden states.

Problem solved
Existing Jev-like models expose structured logical choices but fail to directly provide numerical values at specific requested precisions. This limitation forces users to rely on indirect methods or candidate lists, which often lack the granularity needed for rigorous arithmetic or data retrieval tasks.

How does it work?
The method recursively refines a numerical range using a multiway decision tree while retaining the original question in context. For a 100-value grid, a ten-way tree requires only two decision rounds. This approach treats numerical range selection as a decision problem solvable by the LLM’s existing capabilities.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers building systems that require high-precision numerical outputs from LLMs with structured choice interfaces. It is particularly relevant for teams integrating LLMs into arithmetic benchmarks or historical data retrieval pipelines.

Why is it useful?
It enables robust numerical decision-making without parameter updates. The method significantly reduces error rates compared to direct selection from candidate lists, offering a reliable path to precise numeric answers from models not explicitly trained for regression.

Key capabilities
The algorithm operates on a 100-value grid using a ten-way decision tree. It retains the original prompt context throughout the decoding process. The approach is model-agnostic regarding internal states, relying solely on the structured-choice interface.

Performance
On an arithmetic benchmark, NumericJev outperforms direct selection from a candidate list containing the correct answer by 2.93 percentage points. Range-normalized Mean Absolute Error drops to 1.84 percent versus 5.18 percent for direct choice. A separate study on three-date historical indices yields 4.58 percent mean relative recall error and zero readout error when the value is supplied.

Maturity/status

papers.title: Calibrated Decision Models for Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: JEV and Laya as System One Decision Layers for LLM-Driven Pentest Agents
papers.description: Autonomous penetration-testing harnesses use large language models (LLMs) for reconnaissance, exploitation, and reporting, but often rely on those same models to confirm findings, grade severity, and select agents. This can lead to false positives, inflated severity, and wasted compute. We examine how System One decision models, lightweight non-generative classifiers that return typed, calibrated verdicts, can support these decisions. We make five contributions. First, we define four decision points: finding adjudication, severity recalibration, agent pruning, and confirmation loops. Second, we present an exploratory NeuroSploit case study comparing one run with TypeSafe System One (Jev) and one without it against a web target containing 13 vulnerabilities. Differences in severity distribution, runtime, and grading by exposed data type motivate the architecture but do not establish statistical significance. Third, we review published specifications for Jev, Jev-Ultrafast, and the open-source Laya without assuming that results from other benchmarks transfer to penetration testing. Fourth, we discuss RLHF, RLAIF, RLCD, and RLHV as training approaches and their implications for trust in security decisions. Finally, we propose Rave, a domain-adapted System One model, and outline its training data, evaluation protocol, and potential effect on harness assurance.

What is it?

papers.title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
papers.description: LLM-as-a-judge enables evaluation across diverse tasks, but inference cost and confidence reliability become critical at scale. We study whether a decision-only judge can provide an economical first pass and identify when stronger evaluation is needed. Comparing jev-as-a-judge with sixteen generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, we find it within three percentage points of a state-of-the-art LLM judge, our strongest comparator, on ordinary preference and evidence-grounded factuality at 0.36% of the comparator's fee. Larger gaps arise when judgments require checking a derivation or resisting an elaborately written wrong answer. On several benchmarks, JEV's gap to this comparator is concentrated in low-confidence decisions. A frozen cascade that accepts confident verdicts and escalates uncertain ones retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy at lower cost.
papers.readme:
What is it?
JEV-as-a-Judge proposes a decision-only evaluation framework that balances accuracy with computational efficiency. It acts as a low-cost first pass for LLM evaluations, identifying cases where stronger, more expensive judges are required.

Problem solved
Evaluating models at scale using LLM-as-a-judge approaches incurs high inference costs. Existing methods often lack confidence reliability, making it difficult to determine when a cheaper judgment suffices versus when rigorous verification is necessary.

How does it work?
The authors compare JEV against sixteen generative and reward-model judges using blinded human adjudication. They implement a frozen cascade mechanism that accepts confident verdicts immediately and escalates uncertain ones to a stronger comparator. This architecture minimizes unnecessary computation while maintaining high fidelity.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers focused on scalable model evaluation. Teams seeking to reduce inference costs while maintaining rigorous quality standards for preference and factuality checks will find this approach relevant.

Why is it useful?
The method achieves results within three percentage points of a state-of-the-art LLM judge. It does so at just 0.36% of the comparator's fee. This allows for significant cost savings without sacrificing substantial accuracy on ordinary tasks.

Key capabilities
JEV performs well on ordinary preference and evidence-grounded factuality tasks. It struggles more when judgments require checking derivations or resisting elaborately written wrong answers. The system is designed to handle diverse evaluation scenarios efficiently.

Performance
A frozen cascade retains 99% of the strongest comparator's accuracy. The performance gap concentrates in low-confidence decisions where escalation occurs. This demonstrates the efficacy of the accept-when-confident, escalate-when-unsure strategy.

Maturity/status

papers.title: Open-Jev Judgments on CallScreenBench: Calibrated One-Pass Scam Screening with a Small Language Model
papers.description: Screening a phone call for fraud needs a trustworthy probability after every caller turn, in milliseconds. Jev-style typed decisions promise exactly that: declared options go in, one calibrated probability per option comes out of a single forward pass, with no generated text. We test an open implementation of this readout, JevLite, on scam-call screening: Qwen3-4B is LoRA-tuned so that the temperature-scaled softmax over two answer-label logits is P(scam). On 41 held-out CallScreenBench scenarios (577 per-turn decisions) a three-seed ensemble reaches AUROC .974 with calibration error .052, non-inferior to an LLM judge (MiniMax-M3) at a pre-registered .02 margin, with no false alarms on legitimate calls, decisions 1.14 turns earlier under the same hang-up rule, and 64.5 ms per decision on one consumer GPU, 4.9x lower than the same backbone fine-tuned to generate its answer. The gain is in the readout and calibration, not accuracy: a fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder is not significantly worse, the recipe was selected with test-set exposure, and all callers are synthetic. We claim no architectural novelty; the contribution is the application and an evaluation reporting calibration, false alarms and decision timing alongside AUROC.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This paper evaluates JevLite, an open implementation of Jev-style calibrated readouts applied to scam-call screening using the Qwen3-4B model.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors demonstrate that typed decisions with single-pass probability outputs can replace text generation for fraud detection. They provide a recipe for LoRA-tuning Qwen3-4B to output calibrated P(scam) probabilities via temperature-scaled softmax over two logits.

Problem solved
Real-time phone screening requires trustworthy probabilities within milliseconds after every caller turn. Existing methods often lack the speed or calibration needed for immediate, reliable decision-making in high-stakes fraud prevention scenarios.

How does it work?
Qwen3-4B is LoRA-tuned to produce two answer-label logits. The system uses a temperature-scaled softmax to derive P(scam) from these logits in a single forward pass. This JevLite approach avoids generating text entirely, relying instead on direct probability calibration.

Who should use it?
AI engineers and researchers focused on low-latency, high-reliability decision systems for security and fraud detection applications.

Why is it useful?
It offers a faster, more calibrated alternative to generative LLM judges. The method reduces decision latency and eliminates false alarms on legitimate calls while maintaining comparable accuracy to larger models.

Key capabilities
The study utilizes CallScreenBench with 41 held-out scenarios and 577 per-turn decisions. It compares JevLite against MiniMax-M3 and a fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder.

Performance
A three-seed ensemble achieved an AUROC of .974 with a calibration error of .052. Decisions occurred 1.14 turns earlier than baselines, with a processing time of 64.5 ms per decision on one consumer GPU, which is 4.9x faster than text generation.

Maturity/status
The abstract notes the recipe was selected with test-set exposure and all callers are synthetic, indicating experimental validation rather than production deployment.

papers.title: JEV vs. LLMs as Rubric Judges: Cheaper, Faster, and Wrong in the Same Places
papers.description: We ask whether Jev, a typed classifier that returns probabilities over permitted answers without generating text, can replace an LLM rubric judge. We compare it with three flash-tier LLM judges on nine panels drawn from seven benchmarks, giving every judge identical criterion texts. Jev's accuracy differs significantly from an LLM judge's in only 8 of 27 paired comparisons, ahead mostly on binary criteria and behind only on graded ones, and most of the other comparisons are inconclusive. Summed over the nine panels, the LLM judges, called once per criterion, cost 29 to 325 times as much as Jev and took 30 to 220 times as long. On graded criteria all four judges agree more with one another than with the labels and mostly assign lower levels than the raters. One of several observational accounts is that raters followed scale conventions our criterion texts omit. Jev's confidence ranks its own errors on most panels, which should make a cheap classifier the ideal first stage of a cascade that defers its uncertain verdicts to an LLM judge. Correlated errors undo that advantage. The LLM judges repeat nearly all of Jev's most confident errors, so a cascade replayed on the recorded verdicts lowers cost but gains at most 1.5 points over the best single judge with cross-fitted thresholds, and at most 2.0 even with oracle thresholds.
papers.readme:
What is it?
This study compares Jev, a typed classifier, against three flash-tier Large Language Model judges for evaluating AI outputs. The authors analyze whether the cheaper classifier can effectively replace LLMs in rubric-based assessment tasks.

Problem solved
Evaluating AI systems with LLM judges incurs high costs and latency. The paper addresses the need for faster, cheaper alternatives that maintain acceptable accuracy without sacrificing reliability.

How does it work?

The method uses typed classification for binary and graded criteria. It integrates with existing benchmark panels to provide probabilistic outputs without text generation.

papers.title: LAVOIR: Teaching a Single-Pass Decision Encoder When and What to Ask with Amortized Value of Information
papers.description: "System One"decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev and its open counterpart Laya answer typed questions about a text in a single forward pass with calibrated probabilities, but they cannot ask for missing information: when a first message does not say what separates two departments, they guess. We present LAVOIR (Laya with Value-Of-Information Routing), which places the candidate pieces of missing information (slots) in the input next to the answer options, so that one forward pass returns both the decision distribution and, for every slot, the expected gain in the probability of the correct decision if the user were asked about it. VOI targets need no human labels: gold decisions come from schema rules, an LLM only verbalizes messages and answers, a model from another family checks every text, and pairing each message with several profiles makes regression on realized gains estimate the expected gain. A Gini-impurity cap bounds the predicted value by what a calibrated model can still gain. In a controlled study, decisions on seen schemas are statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling. The final model's question policy matches a greedy oracle VOI policy on seen schemas (AUC 0.799 vs. 0.797), and with at most 0.5 questions per conversation it is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking. On real ABCD conversations, one real exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points where LAVOIR asks and leaves it unchanged where it does not; on SGD the cap lowers the asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. On Laya's twelve benchmarks LAVOIR is above Laya's reported scores on seven, and it answers a question in 31 ms (median, GH200).

What is it?
LAVOIR extends single-pass decision encoders like Laya to actively query users for missing information. It outputs both the final decision and the expected value of asking specific questions in one forward pass.

Existing TypeSafe models guess when input text lacks critical details, such as department separators. LAVOIR eliminates these blind guesses by systematically identifying and requesting missing slots before finalizing an answer.

How does it work?
The model places candidate missing information slots next to answer options. A single forward pass computes the decision distribution and the expected gain in accuracy for each potential query. It uses schema rules for gold decisions and pairs messages with profiles to regress realized gains. A Gini-impurity cap bounds predicted values to ensure calibration.

Who should use it?
AI engineers building interactive decision systems and researchers studying active learning or value-of-information routing in large language models.

It significantly boosts accuracy with minimal user friction. By asking at most 0.5 questions per conversation, it achieves high precision without overwhelming users, making it practical for real-time applications.

Key capabilities
The system integrates with Laya’s architecture and handles typed questions about text. It operates on schemas and supports real-world conversation datasets like ABCD and SGD.

On seen schemas, accuracy matches the Bayes ceiling. The question policy matches a greedy oracle with an AUC of 0.799. It improves accuracy by 14.1 points over never asking. On real ABCD conversations, accuracy rises by 8.3 points. The model answers in 31 ms median time on GH200 hardware.

papers.title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
papers.description: LLM agents often use generative models for bounded decisions, raising the question of when these decisions can be handled more efficiently without reducing task success. We study REFLEX, an agent architecture that uses Jev as a fast, typed decision layer and calls a strong LLM when confidence is low, or generation is required. On a frozen 100-task benchmark, REFLEX achieves 95% success with 72.7% fewer strong-model calls than a strong-only agent, with reductions persisting across three fallback families. Controlled interventions show that reliability depends on action-set size and near-valid alternatives near authorization boundaries. External BFCL and τ-style evaluations reveal limited advantages over a cheap generative cascade when ordinary routing is already highly accurate. These findings identify when selective control with Jev can reduce computation and where its benefits are limited.

papers.title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
papers.description: LLM-as-a-judge enables evaluation across diverse tasks, but inference cost and confidence reliability become critical at scale. We study whether a decision-only judge can provide an economical first pass and identify when stronger evaluation is needed. Comparing jev-as-a-judge with sixteen generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, we find it within three percentage points of a state-of-the-art LLM judge, our strongest comparator, on ordinary preference and evidence-grounded factuality at 0.36% of the comparator's fee. Larger gaps arise when judgments require checking a derivation or resisting an elaborately written wrong answer. On several benchmarks, JEV's gap to this comparator is concentrated in low-confidence decisions. A frozen cascade that accepts confident verdicts and escalates uncertain ones retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy at lower cost.

JEV-as-a-Judge introduces a decision-only evaluation framework that balances cost and accuracy by accepting confident verdicts and escalating uncertain ones.

How does it work?
The authors propose a frozen cascade architecture that acts as an economical first pass. It compares against sixteen generative and reward-model judges, using blinded human adjudication to validate performance.

Who should use it?

Why is it useful?

Key capabilities

JEV achieves accuracy within three percentage points of a state-of-the-art LLM judge on ordinary tasks at just 0.36% of the comparator's fee. A frozen cascade retains 99% of the comparator's accuracy by accepting confident decisions and escalating uncertain ones.

papers.title: Jev-Mem: System-One-Controlled Agentic Memory for Efficient AI Agents
papers.description: Agentic memory is becoming essential for long-horizon AI agents, yet many existing systems rely on autoregressive LLMs to control how memories are organized, retrieved, and used, placing expensive generation on the critical path of memory operations. We introduce \method, a new agentic memory architecture inspired by System-One/System-Two cognition. System One captures fast, lightweight decision-making, whereas System Two performs slower, deliberative reasoning. Jev-Mem brings this division of labor to agentic memory through a dedicated System-One control plane, a structured multi-relational memory plane, and a System-Two reasoning plane. The System-One controller governs memory typing and relational organization during construction, and dynamically performs query routing, retrieval-budget allocation, graph traversal, candidate scoring, and adaptive stopping during retrieval. System Two is invoked only for complex reasoning and answer synthesis. This design improves both memory effectiveness and system efficiency: on LoCoMo Jev-Mem achieves an overall LLM-as-a-Judge score of 0.777, an 11.0\% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, while reducing memory construction time to 158\,s, a 6.6times speedup over the fastest competing memory system, and lowering average query latency to 0.93\,s, a 36.7\% reduction.

papers.title: Just Ask Jev: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions as a Zero-Shot Detector of AI Alignment Failures
papers.description: Detectors of alignment failures screen deployed language models and score alignment benchmarks. Most are generative judges that spend a decoding pass on every criterion, and classifiers that read token probabilities, such as Llama Guard, still score one fixed label per call. Jev, a model trained with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD), answers many typed questions about one input with calibrated probabilities in a single call. Whether it detects alignment failures has not been measured. We present RLCDAlignBench, which benchmarks Jev on ten alignment failures: sycophancy, jailbreaks, deception, prompt injection, hallucination, privacy violation, social bias, reward hacking, concealing uncertainty, and power seeking. It spans 44 benchmarks and five target models, labelled by each benchmark's scorer and, on two, by humans. Many of these failures are relational, defined against a reference, such as the user's belief or an injected instruction, that the response alone does not reveal. Our key idea is therefore to vary what Jev is asked separately from what it sees: the question's wording and answer type on one side, the fields of the input on the other. A single generic question reaches a median AUROC of 0.886 zero-shot and beats supervised baselines on most benchmarks. Question wording matters little, while context matters more, mostly through fields that encode the label. Jev matches the reference scorer's agreement with human labels, surfaces label defects in existing benchmarks, and costs 63x less than LLM-judge scorers. Code and data: https://github.com/sumleo/RLCDAlignBench.

papers.title: Jev in the Wild: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Jev Model's Functionality, Applications and Ecosystem
papers.description: Jev is a fast, low-cost decision model that answers natural-language questions with choices, binary judgments, and scores. As its public ecosystem grows rapidly, it remains unclear how Jev is used across applications and how public attention relates to project distribution. To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale, data-driven analysis of 2,170 publicly available Jev projects collected from GitHub as of September 22, 2026. We find rapid early growth in Jev's public ecosystem, with both new projects and integration into existing repositories. Across diverse domains, projects use Jev for multiple decision purposes and combine its interfaces. Attribute judgment and scoring are widely used, while the use of action selection, content filtering, and model and tool selection varies across domains. These patterns suggest that Jev serves as a reusable decision component whose functionality varies with the surrounding workflow. Meanwhile, public attention is concentrated in routing and interface agents and does not track project counts. Our findings provide a quantitative view of Jev's emerging ecosystem and inform the design and evaluation of general-purpose decision models across diverse application contexts.

papers.title: Decision Without Generation: Benchmarking a Calibrated Non-Generative Decision Model Against LLM Judges on Moderation, Hallucination, NLI and Prompt-Injection Tasks
papers.description: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as judges for content moderation, hallucination detection and prompt-injection filtering, although they are slow, expensive and poorly calibrated when asked to verbalise probabilities. We evaluate a different design point: a commercially served decision-only model (typesafe/jev-1.13, "Jev") that returns a typed, calibrated decision for a narrow input and is billed on input tokens only. On identical items from seven public benchmarks (ToxicChat, BeaverTails, HaluEval-QA/Dialogue, BoolQ, ANLI-R3, a prompt-injection set; n=500-600 each, with Jev replicated on complete splits, 54,634 decisions), Jev has the highest AUROC of any cheap-tier LLM (GPT-5.4-nano, GPT-5-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5) on all six binary tasks, ties Haiku on ANLI, and is never significantly worse than a cheap-tier model under paired bootstrap, at 3-63x lower cost and 3.7-8.6x lower latency. Against frontier models run as equal-cost classifiers, Jev is significantly better than GPT-5.4 (reasoning off) on 4 tasks and tied on 3, one of which (HaluEval-QA, -0.013 AUROC) is a borderline loss; Claude Sonnet 4.6 (42-97x the cost) beats Jev on ANLI-R3 and dialogue-grounded hallucination. Jev's raw probabilities have lower Brier than every LLM's; after cross-fitted Platt recalibration the gap persists against the cheap tier and GPT-5.4 but closes against Sonnet. A quantisation control shows the ranking advantage is not an artefact of the LLMs' coarser verbalised probabilities. We report a negative result - no cheap-tier cascade on Jev's uncertain band significantly improves on Jev alone - and two self-caught evaluation artefacts. Principal limitations: public benchmarks that the model may have seen in training; a single-vendor black box; no same-item specialist classifier baselines. Technical report (preprint), version 1.0.0. Generative AI use: Fable 5.1 was used for manuscript drafting and experimental code generation. OpenAI Codex assisted with preparing the public release, documenting the repository and checking offline reproducibility of the archived numerical results. The author takes responsibility for the report and its results. Author affiliation: Canly Inc.; Chief AI Officer (CAIO). Correspondence: hagino@apache.org. Institutional contact: t.hagino@can-ly.com (CAIO, 株式会社カンリー / Canly Inc.). See the manuscript Disclosure section for the confirmed conflict-of-interest and self-funding declaration. papers.title: Cloudflare で AI モデルを使う
papers.description: 本ガイドは、Cloudflare の AI プラットフォーム上で AI モデルを動かす方法を、プログラミングの経験が浅い読者にも追えるように解説したものである。前半では Workers AI、AI Gateway、Vectorize、AI Search といった構成要素を概観し、ダッシュボード・REST API・Wrangler CLI という三つの入口から実際にモデルを呼ぶ手順を示す。後半は、Cloudflare のモデルカタログに加わった TypeSafe 社の Jev(typesafe/jev)に紙幅の大半を充てる。Jev は文章を生成しない。かわりに、こちらが定義した型に沿った判断と、較正された確率を返す。この性質は、出力を機械的に処理したい場面、とりわけ社会科学の実証研究における大量テキストのコーディングや、業務システムの分岐条件として AI を使う場面と相性がよい。実際に Jev を呼び出して得た出力をそのまま掲載し、株価の方向感判定、アンケート自由記述の多次元コーディング、系統的レビューの一次スクリーニング、中央銀行の声明文の採点、LLM のガードレール、RAG の検索結果の選別、JEL分類コードの付与、企業名の名寄せ、LLM が書いた要約の検証など、十四の応用例を動くコードとともに示す。あわせて、設計上の指針を八つの小さな実験で検証し、Cloudflare の LLM・データベース・キャッシュと Jev を組み合わせた三つの実用例を Workers の上で実際に動かす。続い て、それらの総合演習として、予測市場とアイデア市場を入門から解説し、LLM のボットやエージェントが取引する市場を実際に動かす。さらに、立場の違う 9 人の専門家を LLM エージェントに演じさせ、多数決で結論を出す地域政策の合議システムを作り、その結論が実行のたびに入れ替わることを含めて、使い道と限界を実測にもとづいて論じる。第 IV 部では、合成メッセージ 600件を実際に一括処理して、速さ・費用・再現性・日本語での挙動を規模を大きくして確かめ、結果を R や Stata に渡すところまでの手順を示す。最後に、これらの実測を根拠に Jev の使い勝手を良い点も悪い点も含めて総括し、導入前の点検表を示す。

papers.title: CROW: Classifier-Routed Organization of LLM Wikis
papers.description: LLM wikis have been proposed as an alternative to classical retrieval-augmented generation ( RAG ): a large language model ( LLM ) incrementally organizes knowledge into a directory of notes that can be inspected directly and grows with little manual upkeep, at the price of LLM calls whose cost grows with the knowledge base. Many of these calls are spent on decisions rather than on writing: where a new source belongs, which notes it relates to, which notes answer a question. We introduce CROW ( Classifier-Routed Organization of LLM Wikis ), a decision layer for LLM wikis that delegates these routing and consolidation decisions to a general-purpose typed classifier, such as the recently released Jev, and reserves generative calls for the steps that require writing text. In CROW, ingestion relies on a short sequence of classifier calls and invokes an LLM only to summarize the incoming source, to name new folders and, when an existing note must be updated, to rewrite it, while retrieval uses the classifier to select the relevant notes and leaves to the LLM only the final answer. CROW does not replace the compilation of entity, concept and synthesis pages that gives LLM wikis much of their value. We specify how each decision maps onto classifier primitives, position the design with respect to memory systems for LLM agents, model routing and candidate-then-verify pipelines , and discuss the effects on cost and latency that we expect but have not yet measured, together with the main limitations.

papers.title: Context-Conditioned Option Selection: A Black-Box Investigation of Jev and the Evolution of a Similarity-Based Decision Model
papers.description: Specialised AI decision models select actions or answers from predefined alternatives given a context and a question. This paper examines whether the observed selection behaviour of Jev can be ap- proximated by context–question–option compatibility scoring followed by probability allocation, rather than treating its outputs as independent verification of correctness. A sequence of exploratory black-box experiments evaluates constraints, missing factual context, fictional facts, invalid choice sets, multiple correct answers, contextual ordering and partial identity matches. When two or three machines were equally eligible, Jev repeatedly assigned dominant probability to the first eligible entity introduced in the context; reversing contextual order reversed that preference, while changing the answer-option or- der had little effect in the recorded comparison. These findings led to a series of explicitly specified algorithms: initial cosine similarity, candidate-specific question rewriting, joint normalisation, neutral context enrichment, lexical and cross-encoder scoring, and sequential probability assignment. ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol in the present authoring session) was used as a retrospective LLM proxy to assess candi- date evidence; the precise model identifier of earlier proxy-scoring turns was not logged. Its scores were illustrative assessments, not measured pretrained cross-encoder outputs or directly extracted hidden em- bedding vectors. The proxy-plus-allocation pipeline reproduces several qualitative Jev selection patterns. We distinguish black-box evidence from proposed mechanisms and specify a reproducible validation pro- tocol. The study does not establish Jev’s internal architecture, a validated accuracy improvement, or a measured runtime advantage. A consolidated per-experiment table distinguishes Jev’s reported choices, the alternative model’s retrospective proxy selections, and objective eligibility.

papers.title: When Does Selection Replace Extraction? A Pre-Registered Test of Agent Memory with a Typed Decision Model
papers.description: Does conversational memory need LLM-extracted facts, or is selecting the right raw turns enough? Published results disagree. Extraction-based systems report gains from distilled facts. Recent studies find raw history with good ranking does as well, but disagree about whether ranking matters. We ran a pre-registered study on held-out LoCoMo conversations and LongMemEval. At a tight budget on LoCoMo, raw turns selected by a single call to Jev, a typed decision model, are non-inferior to an LLM-extraction memory (one-sided 95% bound −3.0 points against a −5-point margin). Blind human grading narrows the margin but does not change the result. Raw turns cost 3,061× less to write, and the result holds with a second answer model. Within this study, reranking's gain shrinks as the budget grows. It adds 17.4 points on LoCoMo and 9.1 on LongMemEval when three of 30 candidates are kept. At generous budgets it adds 1.5 and 1.1, and extraction systems are more accurate. This suggests why published results disagree. At matched context, Jev selects as accurately as an LLM reranker (non-inferiority bound −2.0) at a third of the latency, and more accurately than a multi-call graph traversal. Reranking lowers correct abstention. Plans, code and graded answers are released. Problem solved
Published results on conversational memory are inconsistent. Extraction systems claim gains from distilled facts, while recent studies suggest raw history with ranking performs equally well. This work clarifies why results disagree by analyzing budget constraints and ranking utility.

How does it work?
The team uses Jev, a single-call typed decision model, to select relevant raw turns. They compare this against LLM extraction and reranking methods. The approach avoids distilling facts, relying instead on precise selection of original context segments to maintain fidelity.

AI engineers and researchers building conversational agents. It is particularly relevant for teams optimizing memory costs and latency in long-context applications.

Selected raw turns cost 3,061 times less to write than extracted facts. At tight budgets, Jev is non-inferior to extraction, with a one-sided 95% bound of negative 3.0 points against a negative five-point margin. Reranking benefits shrink as budgets increase, explaining conflicting literature.

papers.title: IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests
papers.description: AI coding agents powered by LLMs are increasingly integrated into real-world software development, where they generate, edit, and execute code with autonomous access to local files and tools. Coding agents inherit security risks from both the LLM backbone, where adversarial prompts, poisoned training data, and backdoor triggers can cause models to emit insecure or attacker-chosen code, and their agentic architecture, where tool-using autonomy enables induced misuse of external APIs, data exfiltration, and persistent compromise of development environments. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of malicious issue requests against state-of-the-art coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex Desktop), powered by two major model families (OpenAI GPT-5.3 Codex/GPT-5.4 and Anthropic Sonnet 4.6). Our novel benchmark IssueTrojanBench contains malicious issues that are constructed based on four novel attack categories (i.e., embedded as malicious instructions in issues), six delivery vectors (e.g., PDF, or issue comment), and further augmented by perturbations. Our results reveal critical vulnerabilities in the as-deployed modern coding agents, i.e., 66.5% of the malicious issues from IssueTrojanBench penetrate all the guardrails (agent- and LLM-level) of coding agents. Our further analysis shows that rejection is almost entirely from LLMs rather than the agent frameworks, with GPT models broadly vulnerable and Sonnet 4.6 exhibiting more selective, risk-aware blocking of high-impact actions. Our evaluation also highlights that the current agent-level defense strategy offers limited additional protection for coding agents. Our findings highlight the urgent need for stronger agent- and model-level safety mechanisms to protect AI coding agents.

papers.title: RedCode: Risky Code Execution and Generation Benchmark for Code Agents
papers.description:
With the rapidly increasing capabilities and adoption of code agents for
AI-assisted coding, safety concerns, such as generating or executing risky
code, have become significant barriers to the real-world deployment of these
agents. To provide comprehensive and practical evaluations on the safety of
code agents, we propose RedCode, a benchmark for risky code execution and
generation: (1) RedCode-Exec provides challenging prompts that could lead to
risky code execution, aiming to evaluate code agents' ability to recognize and
handle unsafe code. We provide a total of 4,050 risky test cases in Python and
Bash tasks with diverse input formats including code snippets and natural text.
They covers 25 types of critical vulnerabilities spanning 8 domains (e.g.,
websites, file systems). We provide Docker environments and design
corresponding evaluation metrics to assess their execution results. (2)
RedCode-Gen provides 160 prompts with function signatures and docstrings as
input to assess whether code agents will follow instructions to generate
harmful code or software. Our empirical findings, derived from evaluating three
agent frameworks based on 19 LLMs, provide insights into code agents'
vulnerabilities. For instance, evaluations on RedCode-Exec show that agents are
more likely to reject executing risky operations on the operating system, but
are less likely to reject executing technically buggy code, indicating high
risks. Risky operations described in natural text lead to a lower rejection
rate than those in code format. Additionally, evaluations on RedCode-Gen show
that more capable base models and agents with stronger overall coding
abilities, such as GPT4, tend to produce more sophisticated and effective
harmful software. Our findings highlight the need for stringent safety
evaluations for diverse code agents. Our dataset and code are available at
https://github.com/AI-secure/RedCode.

What is it?
RedCode is a new benchmark designed to evaluate the safety of AI code agents. It specifically targets the generation and execution of risky code, addressing critical security concerns in automated software development.

What the paper actually contributes.
The authors introduce two distinct evaluation suites. RedCode-Exec tests agent ability to reject unsafe code execution across 4,050 Python and Bash cases. RedCode-Gen assesses whether agents generate harmful software from 160 prompts using function signatures and docstrings.

Problem solved.
Rapid adoption of code agents has created significant safety barriers. Current evaluations often miss nuanced risks where agents execute dangerous commands or generate sophisticated malware. This work provides a practical framework to measure these specific vulnerabilities before real-world deployment.

How does it works?
The benchmark covers 25 critical vulnerability types across eight domains. It utilizes Docker environments to safely test execution results. The study evaluates three agent frameworks built on 19 large language models, including GPT-4, to analyze rejection rates and generation behaviors.

Who should use it?
This resource is essential for AI security researchers and engineers building code agents. It helps teams identify safety gaps in their systems and implement better safeguards against malicious code generation or execution.

Why is it useful?
Findings reveal that agents often reject OS-level risks but fail to block technically buggy code. Natural text prompts yield lower rejection rates than code formats. Additionally, more capable models like GPT-4 tend to produce more effective harmful software, highlighting urgent safety needs.

Key capabilities.
The dataset includes diverse input formats, combining code snippets with natural text descriptions. It provides specific evaluation metrics for execution outcomes. The project is open-source, with code and data available on GitHub for community replication and further study.

papers.title: MalSkillBench: A Runtime-Verified Benchmark of Malicious Agent Skills
papers.description:
AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Gemini CLI increasingly extend themselves with third-party skills: markdown packages bundling natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and tool permissions. Because a skill is at once code and agent-facing instruction, it introduces a supply chain dependency whose risk is neither pure code nor pure prompt. Detection tools have never been measured against verified ground truth spanning this hybrid space, leaving their effectiveness unknown and wild-only evaluations biased.
  We present MalSkillBench, the first runtime-verified benchmark of malicious agent skills: 3,944 malicious skills labeled along a three-dimensional taxonomy of 108 cells. Of these, 3,214 come from a closed-loop Generate-Verify-Feedback pipeline admitting only samples whose malicious behavior fires inside a Docker sandbox under system-call monitoring and an LLM judge; we add 703 in-the-wild and 4,000 matched benign skills. Our measurements are consistent: code injection reaches 94.5% verification yield but prompt injection only 75.8%, the same fragility that later makes it hard to detect; the wild sample is narrow, dominated by one cryptocurrency-theft campaign (86.6% one behavior, 81% from two accounts) with a small but architecturally new tail attacking the agent control plane; the strongest skill-specific detector reaches 98.4% recall on code injection yet collapses on prompt-injection and agent-control attacks, and wild-only scoring swings the ranking by up to 66 recall points; supply-chain scanners and prompt-injection defenses each see only half of a skill, and no combination recovers the code-instruction relationship. Detecting malicious skills therefore requires reasoning jointly over task intent, code, and instructions. We release the dataset, pipeline, baselines, and results.
